topics.label: Introduction and learning objectives
topics.groupedBecause: This opening frames the lecture within the cancer course and states what students should learn about cancer causation.

topics.label: Mutation acquisition and clonal evolution in cancer
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how mutations can give cells an evolutionary advantage and how individual circumstances influence their progression towards cancer.

topics.label: Environmental exposures and variation in cancer risk
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine the evidence that environmental exposures influence cancer risk rather than cancer arising solely through unavoidable bad luck.

topics.label: Infectious agents in cancer causation
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how infections can drive cancer, using Burkitt lymphoma to develop the interaction between pathogens and malignant transformation.

topics.label: Mechanisms of environmental DNA damage
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics trace how environmental carcinogens produce DNA damage and mutations, showing how their effects depend on biological processing.

topics.label: Tumour initiation and promotion
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics distinguish mutational initiation from the promotion of tumour growth through a permissive cellular environment.

topics.label: Tissue and developmental susceptibility to carcinogens
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics explain how carcinogenic effects depend on the state of the exposed tissue and consolidate the preceding account of carcinogen specificity.

topics.label: Evidence and methods for assessing carcinogenicity
topics.groupedBecause: These subtopics examine how carcinogenic effects can be detected and attributed to exposures, including the limitations of the available methods.

topics.label: Closing summary and risk–benefit decisions
topics.groupedBecause: This closing draws together the lecture’s conclusions about environmental cancer risks and their assessment through everyday risk–benefit decisions.
